newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS-Polish government approves telecom sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Polish government approves telecom sale.

text.p: The government decided on Tuesday that the long-awaited sell-off of the telecoms monopoly TPSA, Poland's biggest privatisation, will start in 1998 with the flotation of a minority stake in Warsaw and abroad.

"A scheme to sell Telekomunikacja Polska (TPSA), discussed by the cabinet on Tuesday, is the biggest privatisation project so far...and most probably there will never be a larger one," Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told reporters.

The treasury, now TPSA's sole owner, will offer up to 25 percent of its shares on the Warsaw bourse and abroad and the sale may be accompanied by a new issue to increase the company's capital, Telecoms Minister Andrzej Zielinski said.
"We assume that the public offering will be addressed both to retail and institutional investors," he told a news conference after a cabinet meeting.
He said that after the first stage of TPSA's privatisation the state would retain at least a 51-percent stake in the firm.
In the second stage, in which the treasury will reduce its stake to a minority, the government is likely to look for a strategic investor in the company, he said.
"Seeking a strategic investor in the second stage cannot be ruled out, in fact I think it is very probable," he said, adding that the second stage's timetable had not been decided.
The government might also decide on further public offerings of TPSA, either of the treasury's shares or of new shares, should the need arise, he said.

Zielinski said funds from TPSA's new share issues would be spent on the firm's expansion and modernisation and proceeds from the treasury stake's sale would finance vital government programmes, such as its social security reform plan.
Further details of the sale would be worked out by the government in cooperation with a privatisation adviser who would be selected in a tender likely to start in July.
The adviser would assess the value of the company, now estimated at more than $12 billion, and propose how much should be offered for sale, where and when, Zielinski said.
Last year, then privatisation minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek said that if 10-15 percent of TPSA's shares were offered on the Warsaw bourse, this would bring revenues of $2-$3 billion.

First plans to sell TPSA were made in 1991 by a centre-right cabinet but were never implemented because the government was busy fighting an economic crisis that accompanied the 1989 fall of communism.
The coalition of ex-communists and a peasant party, which took over in 1993, delayed a decision on the sale for years.
Some analysts say that only pressure of international institutions and lack of funds to finance reform of the pension system had forced the government to approve the sale now.
Zielinski said he was sure the government formed after parliamentary elections later this year would not abandon plans to sell TPSA, whatever its political complexion.
"Further delay of the privatisation would mean that the company would become increasingly isolated and increasingly less competitive," he said.

Analysts say that the value of TPSA, whose net profit fell to 850 million zlotys ($270 million) last year from 933 million in 1995 due to extensive investment, is set to decline as Poland approaches liberalisation of its telecoms market.
Poland plans to let TPSA's prospective competitors operate lucrative long-distance connections in 1999 and to liberalise international links around 2002.
TPSA, whose revenues increased to 6.7 billion zlotys last year from 5.4 billion in 1995, has doubled the number of telephones in Poland to nearly seven million in four years.
But with a population of 38 million, Poland has one of the lowest rates of phone ownership in Europe.
